ev.jpn_m_taue.text: On rice-planting day the whole village went out to the paddies. Women in matching headcloths pressed seedlings into the mud while musicians on the dykes beat drums so the field kami wouldn't get bored.
ev.jpn_m_snow_roof.text: Overnight the snow buried the house up to the roof. You shovelled all day with a wooden spade, and by evening a tunnel led to the neighbours' door like a burrow.
ev.jpn_m_mochi.text: Before New Year the household pounded rice for mochi in the yard: one swings the heavy mallet, another turns the dough with wet hands between the blows. You got the first hot cake.
ev.jpn_m_bon.text: On the last evening of Bon, lights were set afloat on the river to send the ancestors' souls back. You watched your little lantern bob on the water until you lost it among hundreds of others.
ev.jpn_m_hanami.text: In spring you went to see the cherry trees in bloom by the temple. People sat under them with boxes of food and sake, someone was composing poems, and petals fell right into the cups.
ev.jpn_m_steam_bath.text: The town bath is steam, not water: you sit in a cramped dark room until the sweat pours off you, then rinse it away with hot water. The people on the bench discuss rice prices and other folks' weddings.
ev.jpn_m_tea_bowl.text: A monk served you tea — not a brew of leaves but green powder whisked in a bowl with a bamboo whisk. Bitter enough to bring tears, but afterwards your head is as clear as morning.
ev.jpn_m_junk.text: A Chinese junk with matting sails came into the harbour. Porters carried off bales of silk, crates of porcelain and strings of copper coins, while the sailors shouted to each other in a language nobody around understood.
ev.jpn_m_daibutsu.text: You saw the Great Buddha of Kamakura for the first time — bronze, taller than any house. He sat with lowered eyes, and it seemed he knew everything about you and wasn't angry.
ev.jpn_m_yabusame.text: At the festival of the Hachiman shrine, riders at full gallop shot arrows at wooden targets. Each time an arrow split a board, the crowd gasped as one.
ev.jpn_m_gion.text: At the height of summer the Gion festival floats rolled through the streets of Kyoto — tall as towers, draped in brocade. You could hear the flutes and bells several blocks away.
ev.jpn_m_ramie.text: All winter, while the fields lie under snow, the women spin and weave fine ramie cloth. Your fingers have learned to twist the thread so fine that the old women nod in approval.
ev.jpn_m_squid_lights.text: At night the fishermen went out with torches: the light draws the squid. From the shore it looked as if fallen stars were bobbing on the water.
ev.jpn_m_takuhatsu.text: A begging monk in a straw hat stopped at the gate. He waited silently with his bowl until you put in a handful of rice, then bowed and walked on, his staff jingling.
ev.jpn_m_biwa.text: At the crossroads a blind monk with a biwa lute chanted the tale of the fall of the Taira. When he reached the part where the waves took the child emperor, even the guards wept.
ev.jpn_m_irori.text: On a winter evening everyone gathered round the sunken hearth. A pot of stew hung over the fire, smoke drifted up under the thatch, and the old folk told stories of shape-shifting foxes.
ev.jpn_m_cicadas.text: In summer the cicadas shrilled so loudly you had to shout. You caught them in the temple grove, kept them in a bamboo cage and let them go in the evening.
ev.jpn_m_moon.text: On the fifteenth night of the eighth moon, rice dumplings and autumn grasses were set out on the veranda. Everyone gazed at the full moon and tried to make a poem about it — and nearly everyone did it badly.
ev.jpn_m_kemari.text: In the mansion courtyard young lords in silk robes played kemari: the leather ball must never touch the ground, you keep it up with your feet and count the kicks. The best score of the day was eighty.
ev.jpn_m_takeuma.text: The neighbourhood kids made you a bamboo hobby horse, and you galloped up and down the street on it until you tumbled into a ditch full of water.
ev.jpn_m_two_meals.text: In a samurai house people eat twice a day, in the morning and towards evening. Brown rice, soup, pickles, dried fish; white rice only on feast days. Refusing food or complaining is not done.
ev.jpn_m_miso.text: {npc}, your mother, boiled soybeans for miso, and you mashed them with a pestle in the tub. Then the tub was weighed down with a heavy stone — now you wait until next autumn.
ev.jpn_m_kana.text: A temple monk is teaching you the iroha — the poem in which every syllable appears exactly once. The brush won't obey and the ink runs, but you can already write your own name.
ev.jpn_m_typhoon.text: In autumn a typhoon came. The wind tore the thatch from the roofs, and all night everyone held the doors shut from inside. In the morning the rice lay flattened in the fields and the neighbours' shed was gone.
ev.jpn_m_earth_shake.text: The ground shook so hard the bowls fell off the shelf. The old folk muttered a prayer, gathered up the shards and sat back down to their tea — people here are used to it.
ev.jpn_m_market_day.text: On market day rows of stalls sprang up by the ferry: salt, pots, dried fish, needles, straw sandals. People haggled loudly and paid in Chinese copper coins threaded on a cord.
ev.jpn_m_teppo_thunder.text: Across the river ashigaru were practising with the new teppō guns. The roar sent every crow up from the trees, and stinking white smoke hung over the field for a long time.
ev.jpn_m_nanban.text: "Southern barbarians" walked down the street — Portuguese in enormous breeches, ruffs and feathered hats. A whole crowd of children ran after them, while the grown-ups pretended not to be surprised at all.
ev.jpn_m_kumano.text: A line of pilgrims in white passed the village on their way to the Kumano shrines. There were so many that people call them "a procession of ants". One old woman asked you for water and blessed you for it.
ev.jpn_m_cranes.text: A flock of cranes came down on the harvested fields. They strutted about like lords and called so loudly that you stopped to listen.
ev.jpn_m_odori_nembutsu.text: Wandering monks came to the square and began to dance, striking gongs and chanting "Namu Amida Butsu". People dropped their work and danced along — and so did you.
ev.jpn_m_sumo.text: At the shrine festival the village strongmen wrestled in a ring of heaped sand. The winner got a sack of rice, and the loser laughed louder than anyone.
ev.jpn_m_shojin.text: At the monastery you were served a meatless meal: tofu, mushrooms, lotus root, sesame paste. No fish, no meat — and you ate so much you could barely get up.
ev.jpn_m_paper.text: In winter you made paper from mulberry bark: boiled it, beat it, stirred it into icy water and scooped up a thin layer with a screen. Your fingers went numb, but held up to the light the finished sheet looked like frost.
ev.jpn_m_mass.text: All the Christians of the quarter gathered in the little church for the Christmas service. They sang in Latin without understanding the words, then shared rice and fish at a common table.
ev.jpn_m_hot_spring.text: Up in the hills there is a hot spring: the water smells of sulphur, steam curls above it and snow lies all around. The locals say it heals both the back and the heart.
ev.jpn_d_genpuku.title: Genpuku
ev.jpn_d_genpuku.text: It is time for your genpuku, the coming-of-age ceremony. Your hair will be dressed like a man's, a black eboshi cap set on your head, and you will receive a new, adult name. Whoever puts the cap on you will be your patron for life.
ev.jpn_d_genpuku.lord: Ask the lord of the house
ev.jpn_d_genpuku.kin: Invite an old friend of the family
ev.jpn_d_genpuku.note: Genpuku was the coming-of-age rite for boys of warrior and court families, usually between 12 and 16. The "cap father" (eboshi-oya) was often a powerful patron, and the youth received one character of his name.
ev.jpn_d_genpuku_later.title: The patron's call
ev.jpn_d_genpuku_later.text: {npc}, who put the cap on your head at your genpuku, is going to war and calls you to his retinue. To refuse your "cap father" is to lose him for good.
ev.jpn_d_genpuku_later.go.success: You stayed by his side in battle, and after the campaign he rewarded you generously.
ev.jpn_d_genpuku_later.go.failure: An arrow found you in a skirmish. Your patron sent a physician, but it took you a long time to recover.
ev.jpn_d_nengu.title: More than is due
ev.jpn_d_nengu.text: The jitō steward demands more than is due: "for repairs to the manor", "for a gift to the lord" — and men for labour on top. The old folk remember that on the neighbouring estate the whole village wrote a complaint to the proprietor himself.
ev.jpn_d_nengu.petition: Sign a complaint with the whole village
ev.jpn_d_nengu.petition.success: The proprietor took the village's side: the steward was ordered to return the excess.
ev.jpn_d_nengu.petition.failure: The complaint never arrived. The steward found out who wrote it and took twice as much.
ev.jpn_d_nengu.flee: Leave for the hills with the whole village until he relents
ev.jpn_d_nengu.note: Peasants on medieval shōen estates often complained to proprietors about stewards' abuses. The best-known is the Ategawa petition of 1275, written in kana. Abandoning the village en masse (chōsan) was another form of protest.
ev.jpn_d_ichimi.title: One heart, one water
ev.jpn_d_ichimi.text: At night the village assembly met in the temple. They write an oath to stand together against the lord, burn it, stir the ashes into water and drink from a single bowl: "one heart, one water". The bowl comes round to you.
ev.jpn_d_ichimi.note: Ikki were leagues bound by oath. The ichimi shinsui rite — drinking the ashes of a burned oath — was common in the 15th–16th centuries among village communities, townsmen, minor samurai and followers of the Ikkō sect.
ev.jpn_d_ichimi_later.title: The uprising
ev.jpn_d_ichimi_later.text: The league you swore to has risen: crowds with bamboo spears and sickles march on the lord's manor to demand a lower tax. Everyone looks at you — you drank from that bowl.
ev.jpn_d_ichimi_later.lead.success: The lord gave in and lowered the tax. Every village around is talking about you.
ev.jpn_d_ichimi_later.lead.failure: The lord's warriors scattered the crowd. You were wounded, and your house was searched and stripped of anything valuable.
ev.jpn_d_doso.title: The moneylender
ev.jpn_d_doso.text: There isn't enough money to last until the harvest. The dosō moneylender — a sake brewer with a stone storehouse — lends against pledged goods, but at such interest that the debt grows by half in a year.
ev.jpn_d_doso.note: In the 14th–16th centuries the chief moneylenders of the capital were owners of fireproof storehouses (dosō) and sake brewers. The shogunate taxed them and protected them — until uprisings forced it to proclaim debt cancellations.
ev.jpn_d_doso_later.title: The promissory note
ev.jpn_d_doso_later.text: The moneylender's clerk has come: with interest the debt has doubled. And in the streets people whisper that if everyone rises together, the authorities will proclaim a tokusei — an edict cancelling debts.
ev.jpn_d_doso_later.riot: Join the crowd burning the notes
ev.jpn_d_doso_later.riot.success: The crowd smashed the moneylender's storehouse and burned the debt papers. Your debt is gone.
ev.jpn_d_doso_later.riot.failure: Guards broke up the crowd. You were beaten, and the moneylender kept your pledge and took more besides.
ev.jpn_d_doso_later.work_off: Work off the debt for the moneylender
ev.jpn_d_za.title: The guild
ev.jpn_d_za.text: The za guild of your trade is under the protection of a great temple. Members pay the temple dues, and in return only they may sell these goods in the capital's markets. Outsiders are chased off, or beaten.
ev.jpn_d_za.alone.success: You found buyers around the guild, at the outlying markets.
ev.jpn_d_za.alone.failure: The guild's men overturned your stall and drove you from the market.
ev.jpn_d_za.note: Za were medieval guilds of craftsmen and merchants under the protection of temples, shrines or nobles. They paid their patron and received a monopoly. In the 1570s Oda Nobunaga proclaimed "free markets and free guilds" (rakuichi-rakuza) in his lands.
ev.jpn_d_za_later.title: The guild's share
ev.jpn_d_za_later.text: The guild has won its suit against outside traders, and the patron temple has confirmed its rights. Now it sets the prices, and every member is owed a share.
ev.jpn_d_za_later.share: Take half and give the rest to the journeymen
ev.jpn_d_turncoat.title: A letter at night
ev.jpn_d_turncoat.text: At night a messenger from the neighbouring lord slipped into your camp: if your band changes sides in tomorrow's battle, you will be granted twice the land you hold now. Your own lord knows nothing of the letter.
ev.jpn_d_turncoat.loyal: Burn the letter and say nothing
ev.jpn_d_turncoat.report: Take the letter to your lord
ev.jpn_d_turncoat.report.success: Your lord valued your loyalty and rewarded you generously.
ev.jpn_d_turncoat.report.failure: Your lord smirked: "And why was it you they wrote to?" Now he eyes you with suspicion.
ev.jpn_d_turncoat.note: In the Sengoku period vassals switching sides mid-battle decided many engagements — Sekigahara among them. Lords secured loyalty with hostages and marriage alliances, yet betrayals were constant.
ev.jpn_d_turncoat_later.title: The price of betrayal
ev.jpn_d_turncoat_later.text: Your new lord remembers how you came to him — by treachery. Now he suspects you in turn and demands a member of your household as a hostage.
ev.jpn_d_turncoat_later.flee: Abandon everything and flee to another province
ev.jpn_d_quarrel.title: The insult
ev.jpn_d_quarrel.text: A samurai of a neighbouring house mocked your crest in front of everyone. By the lord's law, both men in a brawl are executed, right or wrong. But if you stay silent, everyone will laugh at you.
ev.jpn_d_quarrel.draw.success: A brief clash, and the offender asked for peace himself. The matter was smoothed over with gifts.
ev.jpn_d_quarrel.draw.failure: You were wounded, and the lord punished you both: part of your stipend was taken away.
ev.jpn_d_quarrel.complain.success: The offender was made to apologise before witnesses.
ev.jpn_d_quarrel.complain.failure: People laughed at you: a samurai running off to complain.
ev.jpn_d_quarrel.note: The house laws of Sengoku lords (such as the Imagawa Kana Mokuroku of 1526) introduced kenka ryōseibai: in a brawl both sides were punished regardless of who was right. Lords used it to stop feuds among their retainers.
ev.jpn_d_nyudo.title: Taking the tonsure
ev.jpn_d_nyudo.text: Many people your age shave their heads and take a Buddhist name without leaving home: they hand affairs to the young and spend their days reading sutras and praying for a good rebirth. A monk you know says you are ready.
ev.jpn_d_nyudo.work: Not yet — there is work to do
ev.jpn_d_nyudo.note: In medieval Japan elderly warriors, merchants and widows often took the tonsure while remaining in the world (nyūdō, "one who has entered the path"; ama, a nun). Even rulers did so: Taira no Kiyomori and many Hōjō regents.
ev.jpn_d_ise.title: Pilgrimage to Ise
ev.jpn_d_ise.text: A guide from the Ise shrines is gathering a group of pilgrims in the village to worship the sun goddess Amaterasu. The whole village saves up for the journey, and those who return talk about it for the rest of their lives.
ev.jpn_d_ise.note: From the 14th–15th centuries the Ise shrines drew ever more common pilgrims. Guides (onshi) toured the provinces handing out charms and organising journeys, and villages formed "Ise confraternities" to save up together for the road.
ev.jpn_d_ise_later.title: The pilgrims' fellowship
ev.jpn_d_ise_later.text: The people you went to Ise with still meet once a month: they reminisce about the road, save for the next pilgrimage, and recently rebuilt a neighbour's house together after a fire.
ev.jpn_d_zazen.title: Sitting in silence
ev.jpn_d_zazen.text: The abbot of a Zen monastery lets lay people join the night sittings. No prayers, no sutras: sit facing the wall and let go of your thoughts. In the morning he sets a riddle: "Two hands clap and there is a sound. What is the sound of one hand?"
ev.jpn_d_zazen.sit.success: Towards morning something in you grew still. You never answered the riddle, but you walked home light.
ev.jpn_d_zazen.sit.failure: Your legs went numb, your thoughts raced, and the master's stick came down on your shoulder twice.
ev.jpn_d_zazen.note: Zen came to Japan from China in the late 12th and 13th centuries (Eisai, Dōgen). Shoguns and samurai supported it, and the "Five Mountains" monasteries of Kamakura and Kyoto became centres of learning and Chinese culture. Kōan riddles belong to Rinzai practice.
ev.jpn_d_nembutsu.title: Namu Amida Butsu
ev.jpn_d_nembutsu.text: At the crossroads a preacher tells ordinary people that neither learning nor rich donations are needed. Say "Namu Amida Butsu" with faith, and the Buddha Amida will receive you into the Pure Land when you die.
ev.jpn_d_nembutsu.argue: Ask what the temples and monks are for, then
ev.jpn_d_nembutsu.note: The Pure Land teachings (Hōnen, Shinran, Ippen) promised salvation to anyone who called on the Buddha Amida's name with faith. In the Kamakura period they spread rapidly among common people, and the Jōdo Shinshū (Ikkō) sect became one of the largest.
ev.jpn_d_child_temple.title: Temple pupil
ev.jpn_d_child_temple.text: The abbot offers to take {npc} as a pupil: the temple teaches reading, sutras and arithmetic. Perhaps one day {g=npc_sex:he|she} will become a learned {g=npc_sex:monk|nun}, or perhaps come home able to read — and that is no small thing.
ev.jpn_d_child_temple.keep: Keep them at home to help
ev.jpn_d_child_temple_later.title: Home for the festival
ev.jpn_d_child_temple_later.text: {npc} came home from the temple for the festival — serious, with neat handwriting and a head full of Chinese characters. The abbot sends word that real scholars are made of such stuff.
ev.jpn_d_child_temple_later.proud: Be proud and bless the studies
ev.jpn_d_child_temple_later.home: Call them home — hands are needed
ev.jpn_d_wako.title: A crew from the islands
ev.jpn_d_wako.text: A crew from the islands is recruiting for a raid on the coasts of Korea and China — over there such men are called wakō, Japanese pirates. They promise plunder in silk and silver. Not all will return.
ev.jpn_d_wako.join.success: The ships came back heavy with plunder. You got a good share — and dreams you would rather not talk about.
ev.jpn_d_wako.join.failure: Troops were waiting on the foreign shore. You came back wounded and empty-handed.
ev.jpn_d_wako.note: The wakō were pirates who ravaged the coasts of Korea and China in the 14th–16th centuries, based on Tsushima, Iki and northern Kyushu; in the 16th century many "Japanese" pirates were in fact Chinese. Suppressing them was the main demand of Ming and Joseon on Japan.
ev.jpn_d_wako_later.title: The search
ev.jpn_d_wako_later.text: Envoys have come from Korea, and the governor of Kyushu has promised to find the men who went raiding. Guards are going door to door, and the neighbours remember where your silver came from back then.
ev.jpn_d_wako_later.temple: Do penance at the temple and give up part of the plunder
ev.jpn_d_tokeiji.title: The divorce temple
ev.jpn_d_tokeiji.text: {npc}, your husband, drinks and raises his hand. The women whisper that a wife can flee to the Tōkeiji convent in Kamakura, and if she lives there as a novice for the set term the marriage is dissolved — the husband cannot take her back.
ev.jpn_d_tokeiji.talk: Talk to him before the elders of the family
ev.jpn_d_tokeiji.talk.success: He was ashamed and promised to change. So far he has kept his word.
ev.jpn_d_tokeiji.talk.failure: The talk ended in shouting. Things at home only got worse.
ev.jpn_d_tokeiji.note: The Tōkeiji convent in Kamakura was founded in 1285 by the widow of the regent Hōjō Tokimune. Tradition says it sheltered wives fleeing their husbands from the start; later the custom became fixed that a woman who lived there for about three (later two) years obtained a divorce.
ev.jpn_d_kamakura_suit.title: A land dispute
ev.jpn_d_kamakura_suit.text: A neighbouring samurai has taken over your holding, citing an old deed. You could go to Kamakura to sue: the shogunate's court settles such disputes under the new code of law, but a verdict can take years.
ev.jpn_d_kamakura_suit.settle: Come to terms and give up part
ev.jpn_d_kamakura_suit.force: Take the land back by force
ev.jpn_d_kamakura_suit.force.success: Your men drove off the neighbour's workers, and he didn't dare argue.
ev.jpn_d_kamakura_suit.force.failure: The clash ended in bloodshed, and word of your high-handedness reached the governor.
ev.jpn_d_kamakura_suit.note: The Kamakura shogunate's court heard vassals' land suits under the Goseibai Shikimoku (1232). Parties exchanged written pleas and evidence; cases could drag on for years, and many vassals were ruined by the trips to Kamakura.
ev.jpn_d_kamakura_verdict.title: The verdict
ev.jpn_d_kamakura_verdict.text: Word has come from Kamakura: the shogunate's court is ready to announce its verdict in your suit. Meanwhile your neighbour, not wanting to wait, offers to make peace and split the disputed land.
ev.jpn_d_kamakura_verdict.hear.success: The court found your deed genuine. The land was returned, and your neighbour was ordered to pay for the harvest.
ev.jpn_d_kamakura_verdict.hear.failure: The court ruled your neighbour's deed older than yours. Years and money wasted.
ev.jpn_d_kamakura_verdict.reconcile: Make peace and split the land
ev.jpn_d_utaawase.title: A poetry contest
ev.jpn_d_utaawase.text: The palace is holding a poetry contest: two teams take turns reciting waka on a set theme, "The moon over a mountain village". The judge names a winner for every pair, and the court will talk about it all year.
ev.jpn_d_utaawase.compete.success: The judge called your poem the best of the evening. People copy it out and pass it from hand to hand.
ev.jpn_d_utaawase.compete.failure: The judge remarked that your moon "shines with borrowed light" — the image was lifted from an old poet. The laughter went on for a long time.
ev.jpn_d_renga.title: Linked verse
ev.jpn_d_renga.text: At a rich merchant's house people have gathered to compose renga — a chain of verses in which each person takes up a neighbour's line and gives it a twist of their own. A hundred stanzas in an evening, and one clumsy line spoils the whole chain.
ev.jpn_d_renga.join.success: Your stanza turned the chain so deftly that the renga master asked you to repeat it. The host invites you back.
ev.jpn_d_renga.join.failure: You faltered, and the master had to rescue the chain.
ev.jpn_d_renga.note: Renga, collective "linked verse", was a favourite pastime of the Muromachi period, bringing together courtiers, samurai, monks and wealthy townsmen. Renga masters such as Sōgi (1421–1502) travelled the whole country.
ev.jpn_d_meibutsu.title: Meibutsu
ev.jpn_d_meibutsu.text: You are offered a meibutsu — a famous Chinese tea caddy once owned by a shogun. The price is what a good estate would cost. They say lords nowadays grant such things instead of land.
ev.jpn_d_meibutsu.refuse: Refuse: a clay pot is a clay pot
ev.jpn_d_meibutsu.note: In the second half of the 16th century famous tea utensils (meibutsu) were valued like land. Oda Nobunaga bought and confiscated them and then granted them to his generals as rewards; Sakai tea masters decided what each piece was worth.
ev.jpn_d_meibutsu_later.title: A lord's eye
ev.jpn_d_meibutsu_later.text: A powerful lord has heard about your tea caddy. His envoy drinks tea at your house, studies the caddy and hints that his master would be pleased to "receive it as a gift".
ev.jpn_d_meibutsu_later.sell: Offer to sell it — at a good price
ev.jpn_d_meibutsu_later.sell.success: The lord laughed and paid twice what you gave. A deal people will talk about.
ev.jpn_d_meibutsu_later.sell.failure: The lord took it as insolence. The caddy was taken, and you were paid a pittance.
ev.jpn_d_meibutsu_later.keep.success: The envoy left empty-handed, and it seems you have been forgotten.
ev.jpn_d_meibutsu_later.keep.failure: The lord remembered the refusal: your house was assessed a "voluntary" war levy.
ev.jpn_d_winter_work.title: The long winter
ev.jpn_d_winter_work.text: The fields lie under snow for almost half the year. Some of the village men go off to neighbouring provinces for winter work — as porters, carpenters, at the salt pans — and come back for the spring ploughing.
ev.jpn_d_winter_work.stay: Stay and weave sandals and mats
ev.jpn_d_fire.title: Fire
ev.jpn_d_fire.text: At night the next quarter caught fire. Wooden houses with paper partitions flare up one after another, and the wind carries sparks straight onto your roof. Neighbours with hooks run to pull down houses in the fire's path.
ev.jpn_d_fire.tear: Pull down houses with the neighbours
ev.jpn_d_fire.tear.success: The fire stopped at the cleared lane. Your house survived, and the quarter will not forget it.
ev.jpn_d_fire.tear.failure: A burning beam crashed down beside you. You were burned, and the house caught all the same.
ev.jpn_d_jizamurai.title: Spear and plough
ev.jpn_d_jizamurai.text: The local lord is recruiting peasants for his army: plough in peacetime, in war a spear and a share of the plunder. Those who distinguish themselves might be entered on the samurai rolls.
ev.jpn_d_jizamurai.note: Until the sword hunt of 1588 the line between peasant and warrior was blurred: well-off villagers (jizamurai) owned weapons, served local lords and led uprisings of their own. Many well-known Sengoku warriors came from such families.
ev.jpn_d_jizamurai_later.title: A name on the roll
ev.jpn_d_jizamurai_later.text: In a skirmish at the ford you held your men when others ran. The lord summoned you and offered to enter your name on the roll of his samurai, with a small fief.
ev.jpn_d_jizamurai_later.land: Take the reward in coin and go back to the land
ev.jpn_d_kanjin.title: The alms collector
ev.jpn_d_kanjin.text: A wandering monk is collecting donations to rebuild a burned temple. Donors' names will be written in a book and read before the Buddha, and the most generous will see their names on a tablet at the gate.
ev.jpn_d_kanjin.note: Fund-raising monks (kanjin hijiri) toured the country collecting money for temples, bridges and roads. The best known is Chōgen, who in 1181–1203 rebuilt Tōdaiji in Nara after the Taira burned it.
ev.jpn_t_ronin.title: Rōnin
ev.jpn_t_ronin.text: Your lord's house has fallen: the castle is taken, he has taken his own life, and his men have scattered. You are left without a master or a stipend — a rōnin, a "wave man".
ev.jpn_t_ronin.new_lord.success: A neighbouring lord took you into service: experienced warriors are in demand these days.
ev.jpn_t_ronin.new_lord.failure: A year of wandering the roads ate up all your savings, and no place was found.
ev.jpn_t_ronin.farm: Settle on the land and plough
ev.jpn_t_ronin.monk: Shave your head and enter a monastery
ev.jpn_t_ronin.note: In the Sengoku period lords died or lost their domains constantly, and their retainers became rōnin, masterless warriors. Some hired on with new lords; others settled in villages or became monks.
ev.jpn_t_ranbo.title: Taking people
ev.jpn_t_ranbo.text: An army passed through the village. The soldiers carried people off — to sell to dealers or hold for ransom; they called it simply "taking people". You were seized with your neighbours and tied to the same rope.
ev.jpn_t_ranbo.ransom: Give everything you have as ransom
ev.jpn_t_ranbo.escape.success: You chewed through the rope and hid in the marsh until dawn. You got home a week later.
ev.jpn_t_ranbo.escape.failure: You were caught by the river. A dealer paid the soldiers for you, and now you have a new master.
ev.jpn_t_ranbo.note: During the Sengoku wars soldiers often carried off civilians (ranbō-dori) and sold them; some captives even ended up with Portuguese slave traders. In 1587 Toyotomi Hideyoshi banned the sale of Japanese abroad.
ev.jpn_t_ranbo_later.title: Hope
ev.jpn_t_ranbo_later.text: The master who bought you has gone bankrupt. He is willing to let you go if you work one more season in his fields without a single complaint.
ev.jpn_t_ranbo_later.buy.success: The master kept his word. You are free again and can go back to your own land.
ev.jpn_t_ranbo_later.buy.failure: The master changed his mind and sold you to a neighbour along with his debts.
ev.jpn_t_yoshi.title: Adopted heir
ev.jpn_t_yoshi.text: A wealthy merchant house with no heir has its eye on you. Here it is customary to adopt a grown young man: he takes the house's name, its shops and storehouses — but to his own family he becomes almost a stranger.
ev.jpn_t_yoshi.accept: Enter the house as its heir
ev.jpn_t_yoshi.note: Adopting adult heirs (yōshi) was common in Japan in both samurai and merchant houses: preserving the house and its name mattered more than blood ties.
ev.jpn_t_ming_voyage.title: A ship to Ming
ev.jpn_t_ming_voyage.text: A ship bearing a "tally" is being fitted out for trade with Ming China. A share is expensive, but swords, copper and sulphur will come back as silk, books and coins — if no storm wrecks the ship and no pirates take it.
ev.jpn_t_ming_voyage.big.success: The ship came back with silk and books. Three times what you put in.
ev.jpn_t_ming_voyage.big.failure: The ship was lost at sea. No cargo, no crew.
ev.jpn_t_ming_voyage.small.success: The ship came back, and your share made a handsome profit.
ev.jpn_t_ming_voyage.small.failure: The ship came back empty: the goods didn't sell in Ningbo.
ev.jpn_t_ming_voyage.note: From 1404 to 1547 Japan traded with China under the tally (kangō) system: ships sailing as embassies to the Ming emperor were fitted out by the shogunate, temples and lords, and merchants of Hakata and Sakai bought shares in them.
ev.jpn_t_great_fire.title: The great fire
ev.jpn_t_great_fire.text: A huge fire has burned out half the town. Your house burned to the ground with all your stores; shacks are already going up on the ashes, and the timber merchants have tripled their prices.
ev.jpn_t_great_fire.leave: Leave and start again somewhere else
ev.jpn_t_great_fire.borrow: Borrow from a moneylender and rebuild fast
ev.jpn_t_accused.title: Trial by boiling water
ev.jpn_t_accused.text: Rice has gone missing from the steward's storehouse, and you are accused. The witness is his own servant. Truth is sought the old way here: before the kami you must plunge your hand into a boiling cauldron and pull out a stone. If there is no burn, you are innocent.
ev.jpn_t_accused.ordeal.success: Your hand turned red, but there were no blisters. The charge was dropped, and the lying servant ran off.
ev.jpn_t_accused.ordeal.failure: The burn was terrible. You were found guilty and made to repay the rice three times over.
ev.jpn_t_accused.note: In the 15th–16th centuries disputed cases were sometimes settled by yugishō, trial by boiling water before the gods: one had to retrieve a stone from a boiling cauldron, and a burn was taken as a sign of guilt. Such ordeals appear in Muromachi diaries and laws.
ev.jpn_t_raised.title: First through the gate
ev.jpn_t_raised.text: When the enemy fortress was stormed, you were the first through the gate. After the battle the lord himself asked your name and had you entered on the samurai rolls with a fief. They say that under this lord even peasants' sons become generals.
ev.jpn_t_raised.accept: Accept the fief and the service
ev.jpn_t_raised.coin: Ask for the reward in silver
ev.jpn_t_raised.note: The Sengoku period was an age of meteoric rises: the best-known case is Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the son of a common ashigaru, who became ruler of all Japan.
ev.jpn_t_coin_jar.title: A jar of coins
ev.jpn_t_coin_jar.text: Digging a hole for a new post, you hit a large clay jar packed to the brim with Chinese copper coins on rotted cords. Someone buried them long ago — and never came back.
ev.jpn_t_coin_jar.keep.success: Nobody found out. You spend the coins a few at a time so as not to raise questions.
ev.jpn_t_coin_jar.keep.failure: A neighbour saw you carrying a heavy sack and informed. You had to share with the steward.
ev.jpn_t_coin_jar.note: Archaeologists have found hundreds of 13th–16th-century hoards of Chinese copper coins in Japan — sometimes a hundred thousand coins in a single jar. Copper from China was the main money of medieval Japan.
ev.jpn_t_tsunami.title: The sea draws back
ev.jpn_t_tsunami.text: After a violent shock the sea suddenly drew back from the shore, baring a seabed full of flapping fish. The old people shouted "Run for the hills!" — and some of the young ones were already going down to gather fish.
ev.jpn_t_tsunami.run: Run for the hills with nothing
ev.jpn_t_tsunami.goods.success: You made it — the water came right up to the edge of your refuge, but no higher.
ev.jpn_t_tsunami.goods.failure: The wave caught you on the path. It threw you onto the slope, barely alive.
ev.jpn_t_tsunami.help: Run to the shore and call people
ev.jpn_t_tsunami.help.success: You dragged several people off the beach, and everyone reached the hill in time.
ev.jpn_t_tsunami.help.failure: The wave knocked you off your feet. You survived by a miracle.
ev.jpn_t_inherit_split.title: Dividing the inheritance
ev.jpn_t_inherit_split.text: The head of the house has left a will, and the lands are being divided among all the children, a piece each. {npc} demands the best plot, by the river: "It was promised to me while the old man lived." The holdings get smaller every generation as it is.
ev.jpn_t_inherit_split.equal: Divide equally as the will says
ev.jpn_t_inherit_split.court: Take the dispute to the shogunate's court
ev.jpn_t_inherit_split.court.success: The court found in your favour. The river plot is yours — and you no longer speak to your own kin.
ev.jpn_t_inherit_split.court.failure: The case dragged on, and half of what was in dispute went on gifts and travel.
ev.jpn_t_inherit_split.note: In the Kamakura period warrior estates were divided among all the children, daughters included. Holdings fragmented, vassals grew poorer, and by the 14th century houses had switched to passing all the land to a single heir.
ev.jpn_j_sam_first.title: First battle
ev.jpn_j_sam_first.text: Your first battle. Before the lines, warriors shout out their names and the names of their forebears. Glory and reward go to the first to cross weapons with the enemy; disgrace on the whole house to anyone who falters.
ev.jpn_j_sam_first.charge.success: You were the first to unhorse an enemy rider. Your lord's scribe entered your name on the list of the distinguished.
ev.jpn_j_sam_first.charge.failure: A spear pierced your armour at the shoulder. You lived, but it will be a long time before your next campaign.
ev.jpn_j_sam_castellan.title: A border estate
ev.jpn_j_sam_castellan.text: Your lord is pleased with your service and entrusts you with an estate on the border: collect the tax, judge the peasants, repair the fortifications and hold out if the neighbour decides to attack.
ev.jpn_j_sam_castellan.warrior: Stay a warrior in the retinue
ev.jpn_j_sam_mongol_reward.title: Reward for the Mongol war
ev.jpn_j_sam_mongol_reward.text: You fought the Mongols and spent your last coins on weapons and men. But after the war there is nothing to share out: no land or plunder was taken from the enemy. The shogunate drags its feet over rewards, and the debts keep growing.
ev.jpn_j_sam_mongol_reward.petition: Go to Kamakura to demand a reward
ev.jpn_j_sam_mongol_reward.petition.succ: Your petition was accepted: you were granted a small holding on Kyushu.
ev.jpn_j_sam_mongol_reward.petition.fail: Months of waiting at the shogunate's gates came to nothing.
ev.jpn_j_sam_mongol_reward.note: After the Mongol invasions were repelled, the shogunate could not reward its warriors properly: a defensive war brought no new land. The warrior Takezaki Suenaga famously travelled to Kamakura himself to press his claim and commissioned a scroll depicting his deeds.
ev.jpn_j_ashi_officer.title: A banner on your back
ev.jpn_j_ashi_officer.text: Your band's captain has been killed, and the commander offers you his men: thirty ashigaru, a banner on your back and the duty to answer for every one of them.
ev.jpn_j_ashi_teppo.title: Teppō
ev.jpn_j_ashi_teppo.text: The band has been issued teppō guns. Match, powder, ball — loud, frightening, and useless in the rain. But a ball pierces armour no arrow can, and you can learn to shoot in a month rather than years.
ev.jpn_j_ashi_teppo.sell: Secretly sell powder on the side
ev.jpn_j_ashi_teppo.sell.success: The powder went to dealers, and nobody noticed.
ev.jpn_j_ashi_teppo.sell.failure: The shortfall was spotted. You were flogged in front of the ranks.
ev.jpn_j_ashi_teppo.note: Portuguese matchlocks reached the island of Tanegashima in 1543. Within a few years gunsmiths in Sakai and Kunitomo were making them, and by the 1570s ashigaru gunners were deciding battles, as at Nagashino in 1575.
ev.jpn_j_smith_blade.title: Tempering
ev.jpn_j_smith_blade.text: A samurai has ordered a blade from you as a gift for his lord. At night, when the colour of the glowing steel shows best, you coat the blade in clay and plunge it into water. One wrong moment and a crack will run along it.
ev.jpn_j_smith_blade.temper.success: A wavy temper line appeared on the blade like a cloud over a mountain. The customer paid double.
ev.jpn_j_smith_blade.temper.failure: A thin ring — and a crack ran down the blade. A month of work wasted.
ev.jpn_j_smith_blade.master: Call the old master and learn
ev.jpn_j_smith_ming.title: Swords for China
ev.jpn_j_smith_ming.text: Merchants from Hakata and Sakai are buying swords by the thousand for the ships to Ming, where Japanese blades fetch a high price. You can forge fast and many, or slow and well.
ev.jpn_j_smith_ming.note: Swords were Japan's chief export to China: single 15th-century embassies carried tens of thousands of blades. Mass production lowered their quality, and Ming officials complained about it more than once.
ev.jpn_j_craft_workshop.title: A business of your own
ev.jpn_j_craft_workshop.text: The old master you trained under is retiring. He offers you the workshop with its apprentices, customers and guild seat — in return for a share of the income as long as he lives.
ev.jpn_j_sake_sour.title: The sake is souring
ev.jpn_j_sake_sour.text: In summer a batch of sake began to sour. You could pour it all away and lose the money, water it down and sell it as it is, or try the method of Nara's brewing monks — heating the sake so it won't spoil.
ev.jpn_j_sake_sour.heat.success: The sake stopped souring and kept until autumn. Now you know the secret.
ev.jpn_j_sake_sour.heat.failure: You overheated it — the sake went cloudy and bitter. It had to be poured away.
ev.jpn_j_sake_lender.title: A pawnshop
ev.jpn_j_sake_lender.text: Neighbours keep asking you for loans against pledges: brewers have both money and a stout storehouse. You could open a pawnshop at the brewery, as the richest brewers of the capital do. Only, in uprisings such shops are the first to be smashed.
ev.jpn_j_sake_lender.note: In the Muromachi period sake brewers (sakaya) and storehouse owners (dosō) were the chief moneylenders. The shogunate taxed them, and rebelling peasants smashed their storehouses demanding debt cancellations.
ev.jpn_j_noh_patron.title: Before the shogun
ev.jpn_j_noh_patron.text: Your troupe has been summoned to perform before the shogun and his guests. Please him and the troupe has a patron for years; fail and the doors of the great houses will be shut for a long time.
ev.jpn_j_noh_patron.bold: Play it new, as no one has before
ev.jpn_j_noh_patron.bold.success: When you froze in your mask in the middle of the stage, the hall held its breath. The shogun sent the troupe silk and silver.
ev.jpn_j_noh_patron.bold.failure: The novelty was thought impudent. The guests whispered, and the shogun left before the end.
ev.jpn_j_noh_patron.classic: Play it the way you were taught
ev.jpn_j_ama_storm.title: One more dive
ev.jpn_j_ama_storm.text: Clouds are gathering over the sea, and you have just found a rock on the bottom covered in big abalone. One more dive and the basket will be full.
ev.jpn_j_ama_storm.dive.success: The basket is full, and you reached the boat before the first wave.
ev.jpn_j_ama_storm.dive.failure: The current dragged you under a rock. They pulled you out unconscious.
ev.jpn_j_tea_lord.title: Tea for a lord
ev.jpn_j_tea_lord.text: A lord said to burn temples and execute without trial wishes to come to you for tea. A cramped hut, a single flower in a vase, a plain bowl — and him without his sword: by custom swords are left at the entrance.
ev.jpn_j_tea_lord.simple: Receive him simply, like any guest
ev.jpn_j_tea_lord.simple.success: The lord sat silent over the bowl for a long time, then said: "Here I have rested." Now you are in his service.
ev.jpn_j_tea_lord.simple.failure: The lord felt he was being received like a commoner. He left without finishing his tea.
ev.jpn_j_tea_lord.lavish: Bring out your finest Chinese utensils
ev.jpn_j_tea_lord.note: In the second half of the 16th century the tea ceremony became part of politics: Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi kept Sakai tea masters at their side — Imai Sōkyū, Tsuda Sōgyū, Sen no Rikyū. The wabi style prized simplicity and poverty above luxury.
ev.jpn_j_merchant_ship.title: A junk of your own
ev.jpn_j_merchant_ship.text: An old shipmaster is selling his junk along with the crew. With it you could carry goods to Korea or across the Inland Sea yourself, instead of paying others for every bale.
ev.jpn_j_sohei.title: The monks of Mount Hiei
ev.jpn_j_sohei.text: The monks of Mount Hiei are coming down into the capital again with a portable shrine to press their demands on the court. Hooded warrior monks carry naginata; whoever touches the shrine brings down the wrath of the gods.
ev.jpn_j_sohei.join.success: The court gave way, and you returned to the mountain victorious.
ev.jpn_j_sohei.join.failure: The shogun's warriors met the procession with arrows. You were wounded at the palace gate.
ev.jpn_j_sohei.note: The great monasteries — Enryakuji on Mount Hiei, Kōfukuji in Nara — kept bands of armed monks (sōhei) and repeatedly marched on the capital with portable shrines (gōso) to pressure the court. Enryakuji's power ended when Oda Nobunaga burned it in 1571.
ev.jpn_j_scribe_bugyo.title: A post in the office
ev.jpn_j_scribe_bugyo.text: The office needs someone who knows the law and can draft rulings in lawsuits. The post brings a salary and standing — and enemies among those who lose their cases.
ev.jpn_j_kannushi_fest.title: Whose palanquin
ev.jpn_j_kannushi_fest.text: The shrine's autumn festival is coming. Two villages are arguing again over whose turn it is to carry the kami's palanquin, and threaten not to come at all.
ev.jpn_j_kannushi_fest.lot: Decide by lot before the altar
ev.jpn_j_kannushi_fest.lot.success: Both sides accepted the lot: it is the will of the kami. The festival went well.
ev.jpn_j_kannushi_fest.lot.failure: The losers shouted that the lot was rigged and walked out.
ev.jpn_j_kannushi_fest.both: Have a second palanquin made at the shrine's expense
ev.jpn_j_kannushi_fest.big: Give the honour to the richer village — it gives more
ev.jpn_j_farm_seed.title: Red rice
ev.jpn_j_farm_seed.text: A trader has brought seed of "red rice" from overseas — hardy, quick to ripen and unafraid of drought. It tastes worse, but the harvest is surer. The old men grumble that it has never been done this way.
ev.jpn_j_farm_seed.plant: Sow it on the far field
ev.jpn_j_farm_seed.plant.success: In a dry summer your red rice thrived while everything of your neighbours' withered.
ev.jpn_j_farm_seed.plant.failure: The rice grew, but there was nobody to sell it to — no one wanted it.
ev.jpn_j_farm_seed.note: From the 14th century "red rice" (taitōmai), a hardy variety from China and Southeast Asia, spread in Japan. Together with double cropping (rice in summer, barley or wheat in winter) it helped the population grow.
ev.jpn_j_fish_boat.title: A shoal out at sea
ev.jpn_j_fish_boat.text: An old fisherman says he saw from the hill that the water is boiling far offshore — a big shoal is running. The boats are small, and the wind may turn by midday.
ev.jpn_j_fish_boat.far.success: The nets nearly split. The whole village ate fish for a week, and the rest went to market.
ev.jpn_j_fish_boat.far.failure: The wind turned and the boat capsized. You swam to shore, but the gear was lost.
ev.jpn_j_fish_boat.near: Fish near the shore, as always
ev.jpn_mv_capital.title: To the capital
ev.jpn_mv_capital.text: A man from your parts has come back from Kyoto full of stories: there is work for everyone — in the silk workshops, at the temples, in markets selling goods from all over the world. He asks you to come along.
ev.jpn_mv_kamakura.title: The shogun's town
ev.jpn_mv_kamakura.text: In Kamakura, at the shogun's seat, people are needed: warriors for the retinue, carpenters and carvers to build the new temples. They say there they look at what you can do, not at your pedigree.
ev.jpn_mv_kamakura.note: After 1185 Kamakura, the headquarters of Minamoto no Yoritomo and the Hōjō regents, became the country's second centre: the shogun's vassals, litigants, craftsmen and monks from China gathered there.
ev.jpn_mv_sakai.title: A free city
ev.jpn_mv_sakai.text: A trader you know invites you to Sakai: the city is its own master, ringed by a moat, lords have no say there, and ships from China and the southern seas come into the harbour. You can set up a business there faster than anywhere.
ev.jpn_mv_sakai.note: In the 15th–16th centuries Sakai was run by a council of wealthy townsmen (egōshū), surrounded by moats, and hired its own guards. Missionaries compared it to Venice.
ev.jpn_mv_onin_flee.title: Fleeing the capital
ev.jpn_mv_onin_flee.text: The war is tearing the capital apart block by block. Neighbours load their belongings onto carts: some to Sakai, still quiet for now, some to distant kin in the provinces. Court poets and craftsmen are leaving for the castles of provincial lords.
ev.jpn_mv_onin_flee.stay.success: Your quarter survived — by a miracle, between two burned-out districts.
ev.jpn_mv_onin_flee.stay.failure: Mercenaries broke into the house at night. You came out alive, but with nothing left.
ev.jpn_mv_onin_flee.note: During the Ōnin War (1467–1477) many people of Kyoto, including courtiers and monks, fled to the provinces. That is how the culture of the capital — poetry, tea gatherings, painting — spread to the castles of provincial lords.
ev.jpn_mv_port.title: To the sea
ev.jpn_mv_port.text: A carter says the big harbour needs rowers, porters and carpenters — ships leave for Korea and China, and they pay in hard coin, not rice.
ev.jpn_mv_home_village.title: Into the snow country
ev.jpn_mv_home_village.text: The city has worn you out: fires, wars, noise, endless debts. An acquaintance from Echigo invites you north — it is quiet there, the snow is waist-deep, and a plot of land costs little.
ev.jpn_mv_home_village.go: Move to Echigo to live out your days in peace
ev.jpn_f_misogi.title: Purification
ev.jpn_f_misogi.text: The shrine priest invites you to misogi, purification: at dawn you stand under an icy waterfall and recite the prayer until you no longer feel the cold. They say the water washes away both dirt and misfortune.
ev.jpn_f_misogi.go.success: At first it took your breath away, then everything grew still and bright. You walked home as if reborn.
ev.jpn_f_misogi.go.failure: The purification ended in two weeks of fever and coughing.
ev.jpn_f_pure_land.title: Kami or Buddha
ev.jpn_f_pure_land.text: Your neighbours go to the Pure Land temple more and more. The old preacher says: "The kami can help with the harvest, but after death only Amida Buddha can save you." And the shrine priest is offended that the offerings have dwindled.
ev.jpn_f_pure_land.accept: Put your trust in Amida Buddha
ev.jpn_f_pure_land.kami: Hold to the kami of your forebears
ev.jpn_f_pure_land.both: Go to both — like everyone else
ev.jpn_f_pure_land.note: Most Japanese revered both kami and buddhas: kami were thought of as local manifestations of buddhas (honji suijaku). But Pure Land preachers taught reliance on Amida alone, so a choice between temple and shrine still had to be made.
ev.jpn_f_rain_kami.title: Praying for rain
ev.jpn_f_rain_kami.text: The drought is in its third month. The Buddhist services have not helped, and the village is going to the shrine of the mountain kami with offerings to ask for rain the old way, with dances and drums.
ev.jpn_f_rain_kami.go: Go to the kami with everyone
ev.jpn_f_rain_kami.sutra: Recite the rain sutra at the temple
ev.jpn_f_rain_kami.well: Dig a new well while the others pray
ev.jpn_f_jesuit.title: Bateren
ev.jpn_f_jesuit.text: In the street a man in a black cassock — a "bateren", as they call the padres here — speaks through an interpreter of a single Creator God, "Deusu", before whom all are equal. The mission tends the sick and feeds the poor.
ev.jpn_f_jesuit.refuse: Walk away: we have our own gods
ev.jpn_f_jesuit.note: The Jesuit Francis Xavier landed at Kagoshima in 1549. Within half a century, by the missionaries' estimates, up to 300,000 Japanese had become Christians (Kirishitan), most of them on Kyushu. Converts included lords such as Ōtomo Sōrin, Ōmura Sumitada and Arima Harunobu.
ev.jpn_f_jesuit_later.title: Disfavour
ev.jpn_f_jesuit_later.text: The authorities have turned against the Christians: churches are being closed, the padres ordered to leave, and the neighbours eye your rosary and cross.
ev.jpn_f_jesuit_later.renounce: Renounce it and return to the faith of your forebears
ev.jpn_f_jesuit_later.open.success: You were left alone. And a few neighbours came secretly to ask you about your faith.
ev.jpn_f_jesuit_later.open.failure: You were seized and held in prison until someone paid for your release.
ev.jpn_f_nichiren.title: The Lotus Sutra
ev.jpn_f_nichiren.text: A monk of the Nichiren school beats a drum at the crossroads, shouting that all other teachings lead to hell and only the Lotus Sutra can save the country. The crowd laughs one moment and grows angry the next, and some repeat after him: "Namu myōhō renge kyō."
ev.jpn_f_nichiren.argue.success: You stumped the monk, and the crowd murmured approval.
ev.jpn_f_nichiren.argue.failure: The monk out-argued you in front of everyone. People laughed at you.
ev.jpn_f_nichiren.note: Nichiren (1222–1282) taught that salvation lay in the Lotus Sutra alone and fiercely attacked other schools. His followers were especially strong among the townspeople of Kyoto; in the 1530s their "Lotus leagues" effectively ran the capital.
ev.jpn_f_yamabushi.title: The mountain ascetic
ev.jpn_f_yamabushi.text: A yamabushi — a mountain ascetic in a short cloak, with a conch-shell trumpet — invites anyone willing to join a pilgrimage to the holy mountain: a week of climbing over rocks, fasting, night prayers by the waterfalls. They say whoever completes it gains strength.
ev.jpn_f_yamabushi.go.success: You came back thin but tough as a pine root.
ev.jpn_f_yamabushi.go.failure: You slipped on a wet path and hurt your leg.
ev.jpn_f_yamabushi.note: Shugendō, the way of the yamabushi mountain ascetics, blended Buddhism, kami worship and ancient mountain cults. Yamabushi led pilgrims to the holy mountains of Yoshino, Kumano, Haguro and others.
